notation.meaning: Standard deviation of the errors and its estimate
A random variable with the $t_{N-K}$ distribution
Number of parameters and of observations

blocks.md: A regression gives one estimated slope, but a different sample would give a different one. A hypothesis test asks whether the estimate is far enough from some claimed value that chance alone is an unlikely explanation. Distance is measured in standard errors: an estimate two or more standard errors from the claimed value is usually judged too far. A two-sided test asks "is the slope different from the claim?"; a one-sided test asks a directional question such as "is the slope larger?" and puts all of its doubt in one tail.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Every regression table prints a test of "is this coefficient zero?", and exam questions turn on choosing the right null, the right tail and the right standard error.
Under SR1 to SR6 (or approximately, in large samples), for the null $H_0: \beta_k = c$:

| Alternative | Reject $H_0$ at level $\alpha$ if | p-value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $H_1: \beta_k \neq c$ (two-sided) | $\lvert t\rvert > t_{1-\alpha/2,\,N-K}$ | $2\,P(T > \lvert t\rvert)$ |
| $H_1: \beta_k > c$ (right tail) | $t > t_{1-\alpha,\,N-K}$ | $P(T > t)$ |
| $H_1: \beta_k < c$ (left tail) | $t < -t_{1-\alpha,\,N-K}$ | $P(T < t)$ |

- **Default two-sided test of $\beta_2 = 0$**: $t = 10.21/2.093 = 4.88 > 2.024$, $p < 0.001$. Reject: income is related to food spending.
- **One-sided test of $\beta_2 = 7$ against $\beta_2 > 7$** (the critical value is beyond what the lecture prints): $t = (10.21 - 7)/2.093 = 1.53 < t_{0.95,38} = 1.686$, right-tail $p = 0.067$. Do not reject at 5%: the data are consistent with 7 cents of each extra dollar going to food.
- **Link to intervals**: the 95% confidence interval [5.97, 14.45] excludes 0 and includes 7, which agrees with both two-sided conclusions.

- **Wrong row.** The intercept's p-value (0.062 in the food table) says nothing about the slope.
- **Wrong critical value.** A one-sided 5% test uses the 0.95 quantile (1.686 with 38 df), not 2.024. Decide the alternative before looking at the estimate.
- **"Fail to reject" is not "accept".** The test keeps $H_0$ as a possibility; it does not show $H_0$ is true.
- **Statistical is not economic significance** (beyond the lecture). With 526 workers, the wage-on-experience slope of \$0.031 an hour per year of experience has $t = 2.60$, yet it is tiny in dollars and the regression's $R^2$ is 0.013 ([Coefficient of Determination](note:coefficient-of-determination)). Report the size of an effect as well as its p-value.
- **Mixing $\sigma$ and $se$.** The standard error already includes the estimate of $\sigma$; that is why the reference distribution is $t$, not normal.

- Econometrics: every coefficient in a regression table; confidence intervals are the same calculation turned around ([Confidence vs Prediction Intervals](note:confidence-vs-prediction-intervals)).
- Diagnostics: tests such as Jarque-Bera and Breusch-Pagan follow the same logic with other statistics ([Regression Diagnostics](note:regression-diagnostics)).

The same $t$ test handles one restriction on several coefficients, such as $H_0: -0.4\beta_2 + 0.8\beta_3 = 0$ for a burger chain's marketing plan ($t = 6.56$); its standard error needs the covariance of the estimates ([Delta Method](note:delta-method)). Several restrictions at once need the [F Test of Joint Hypotheses](note:f-test-of-joint-hypotheses).
